name: ThermiVa

lead: ThermiVa is a branded non-invasive radiofrequency treatment from Thermi Aesthetics that heats vulvovaginal tissue under physician control to stimulate collagen. Clinics offer it for vaginal laxity, a more youthful-appearing vulva and related concerns.
One sham-controlled trial, the TIGHT study, tested it in 63 women, and a review described promising early results.

paras: It is an in-office procedure, with sessions around 30 minutes and no downtime according to Grokipedia, using a handpiece that heats tissue to roughly 40 to 45 degrees C. A series of sessions is typical.

Grokipedia lists transient pain, redness and swelling as side effects. In 2018 the FDA cautioned that safety and effectiveness of energy-based vaginal devices had not been well established and wrote to manufacturers, and an analysis of MAUDE reports characterized adverse events.

angle.text: Clinics use controlled heating to stimulate collagen, hoping for tighter tissue and a more youthful-looking vulva.

lead: ThermiVa is a non-ablative, temperature-controlled radiofrequency treatment delivered to the vulvovaginal region, marketed for tissue tightening, a more youthful vulvar look, and symptoms such as laxity. [1][2]

A 2016 review described transcutaneous radiofrequency in this area as showing promising results for appearance, elasticity, stress urinary incontinence and sexual function. [2] The TIGHT study, a prospective sham-controlled randomized trial at three sites in Australia and India, enrolled 63 parous women with vaginal laxity (34 treatment, 29 sham). [3]
A 2020 analysis of FDA MAUDE reports noted the FDA had cautioned that safety and efficacy of energy-based vaginal devices had not been well established and had sent letters to manufacturers. [4]

paras: Grokipedia describes ThermiVa as physician-controlled radiofrequency energy delivered by a handpiece, requiring no anesthesia and no downtime. [1] It reports the US system is cleared as an electrosurgical device and Europe indicates it for vulvovaginal laxity. [1]
The 2020 MAUDE analysis reviewed adverse events and noted observational data were limited. [4] Grokipedia lists transient pain, erythema and edema, and contraindications such as pregnancy. [1]

The TIGHT study was a prospective single-blinded sham-controlled trial of 63 women; treated participants had an 8-point mean improvement in FSFI scores at 3 months. [3] A 2016 review summarized earlier results. [2]

timeline.event: FDA cautions that safety and efficacy of vaginal energy-based devices are not well established (July 30 warning referenced in a 2020 analysis). [4]
